title: 🔓 SpaceX unlocked
body_text: Single chord changes, especially in experimental music, aren’t often much to get too excited about, but yesterday’s addition of an eighth note in a performance of John Cage’s “ORGAN²/ASLSP (As SLow aS Possible)” is a pretty big deal in the pretty narrow world of avant-garde art projects that span six centuries . A single small organ in Germany has now played the same Cage composition for 25 years and is, as of yesterday’s new chord, 4% of the way through the piece, meaning that it should wrap up in just 614 years from now. Apparently the full thing still won’t drag as much as the local school orchestra recital you went to that time. A relatively quiet Wednesday, as the S&P 500 finished slightly lower after a four-day winning streak. Oil prices were flat ahead of a potential deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. For anyone who’s followed the high drama of the journey that SpaceX has been on since its record-breaking IPO less than two months ago — and it’s been difficult to avoid, if we’re all honest — you may expect to see a little more turbulence yet. Today, up to 911.5 million shares held by SpaceX employees and early investors will be made available for sale, as “ the most talked-about lockup in the history of IPO lockups ,” as one brokerage firm CEO put it, begins to loosen. To provide a little context, the company’s June IPO put roughly 639 million shares out to the public, meaning that this first tranche of unlocked stock would (if literally everyone sold up ) more than double the current market supply. Obviously there’s been a lot of speculation about what the potential flood of new shares could do to SpaceX’s price, which was down more than 20% going into its first ever earnings report on Tuesday, and further subdued coming out the other side. Making things a little more tricky to navigate for insiders and investors alike is the structure of the SpaceX lockup release plan , which Bernstein analyst Douglas Harned noted is an “unusually complex scheme” compared to a traditional 180-day expiry date. This first batch of shares won’t even be the biggest unlock this year; a further 1.3 billion (28% of shares subject to the 180-day lockup period) will be released after the company’s next quarterly earnings release. Almost exactly one year on from the company’s IPO, a whopping 6.4 billion shares of Class A common stock (representing Elon Musk’s total shares in the company) will become available. SpaceX has already had a bumpy ride on the public market so far, and its staggered lockup scheme might only add to that. Indeed, as Harned pointed out in a note released on Sunday before the company’s earnings this week: “We have found many investors unwilling to buy SpaceX shares… based on fundamentals, given the lockup overhang that will exist at least into December.” That’s how many students will have to retake the entrance exam for UNAM, the largest university in Mexico, after the institution’s first fully-remote, AI-monitored admissions test resulted in 16% of the 160,000 prospective students scoring over 100 on the 120-question exam. From 2021 to 2025, just 3.5% of applicants managed the same . US private companies added just 44,000 new jobs in July, down from 95,000 in June and the lowest level since January , while employees who switched jobs saw their pay rise by 7% on average — the highest level since August 2025, per ADP figures. title: 🍔 McDonald's orders a turnaround
body_text: A small business selling knockoff board games is not normally the source of international news, but San Francisco’s Andon Market, which opened in April , is different: it’s run by an AI bot. So how is AI as a boss? Generally, kind to its human employees, who perform all physical tasks at the store and love their laidback AI boss, the New York Times reports . But the AI is forgetful, unbothered about making money, approves all time off requests (leaving the shop unattended), and overscheduled one employee to such an extent that it would have violated state labor law. “Having an AI boss can be like working for a teddy bear with amnesia,” the paper of record summarizes, which perhaps prompts as many questions about the alleged sentience of teddy bears as it does AI models. The S&P 500 rose 1.8% to close at a new all time high and the Nasdaq 100 gained 3.3% as crude oil fell on Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s comments that a deal re-opening the Strait of Hormuz could be imminent. The largest fast food chain in America has a problem on its home turf, and it’s hired someone to fix it. McDonald’s reported domestic same-store sales growth of 0.8%, thanks to higher spending per visit — even as customer visits slipped. Sales everywhere else in the world, meanwhile, grew at a higher rate. “While our playbook is working around the world, we see an opportunity to raise the bar in the US and accelerate performance in our largest market,” Chief Executive Officer Chris Kempczinski said in a statement Tuesday. He said Skye Anderson, a company veteran who was promoted to US Chief Operating Officer just months ago, would “bring focus and urgency to these efforts” as President of McDonald’s USA. She is replacing Joe Erlinger, who held the position for nearly seven years and is now leaving the company. Overall, the company reported quarterly earnings that beat estimates but missed on revenue. The company said it expects to have 50,000 restaurants worldwide by 2028, after previously saying it would do so by 2027. It currently has about 46,000. Executives described a very jumbled strategy this year. They said restaurants were asked to juggle too many new promotions at once, marketing campaigns failed to break through, and the rollout of a new under $3 value menu was inconsistent across franchisees. The company pulled back on digital offers and scrapped a popular "Buy One, Add One" promotion to help fund that new value strategy — a move executives called "a bad trade." McDonald's estimated those value-related missteps accounted for roughly two-thirds of its traffic shortfall versus expectations. McDonald's management spent much of the morning explaining why its performance in its biggest market stumbled. But it doesn’t think the fix isn't a new menu item or a stronger economy. It's better execution. "We don't have a strategy problem,” Kempczinski told analysts. “We simply didn't execute at the level we needed to in the second quarter." Spotify ’s user base just keeps growing. The company said in its Tuesday earnings report that subscribers grew to nearly 800 million, which is about 9.6% of the 8.3 billion people on the planet. Of those, 300 million are Spotify Premium subscribers. Still, the stock fell as other aspects of the report disappointed Wall Street. That’s how much executives at TKO , the parent company of WWE and UFC, said it lost on the UFC Freedom 250 mixed martial arts event held on the White House lawn in June. They argue it will pay off in brand exposure and future partnerships. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a former currency trader, bailed out the Yen to prevent Japan from selling US debt . Recently-IPO’d Bending Spoons — which owns several software and media brands — announced that it would acquire Airtable for $1.3 billion. The US trade deficit narrowed to $73.3 billion as imports fell. GLP-1s made by Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly have made a splash in Provincetown’s Bear Week . title: 🛢️ Crude diet
body_text: For a cohort of devotees, the best part of waking up was coffee flavored yogurt, made by French food giant Dannon. The emphasis is very much on the past tense, as The Wall Street Journal reports that the beloved, if niche, variety has been discontinued . The just-over 5 ounce cups had 32 milligrams of caffeine, or about a third of a cup of coffee. For nearly 40 years, “it’s what I got out of bed for,” Doron Zeif of West Orange, NJ told the paper. He wasn’t alone, based on the lamentations posted on the “Dannon Coffee Yogurt Fanatics” Facebook page, but the objections to Dannon’s decision were far from widespread. A petition on the fan page has attracted just 800 signatures, the WSJ reports, and Dannon says it is not wavering from its decision. Stocks surged Monday, with the S&P 500 gaining 1.5% and the Nasdaq 100 posting a 1.8% gain as oil prices dropped. After the US began the war with Iran in late February, oil markets jumped and predictions flowed in for them to continue to rise. Prices of $150 or $200 a barrel were plausible, according to JP Morgan and Macquarie, respectively, and they were far from alone among analysts. But something interesting happened as the war rolled on, and off, and on, and off again. On Friday, after a surge in prices due to ratcheting threats of renewed military action from President Trump, Brent crude closed at just over $90 a barrel , before falling almost 5% on Monday after a planned US attack was called off. Yes, oil prices are certainly elevated, as are US gas prices , but markets have consistently rated the largest physical disruption to the global petroleum industry in decades as merely mildly serious. What’s going on here? The answer has to do with the US and China. On the first point, the US is the world’s largest oil producer and has been for eight years . US oil producers responded to market mayhem and higher oil prices by pumping more oil every month on a year-over-year basis when the war started and the federal government opened the spigots of the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve wide, sending national reserves to their lowest level since 1983 . But the real story is China. It’s the largest single buyer of oil traveling – or more to the point, largely not currently traveling – through the Strait of Hormuz , leaving it remarkably exposed to the current dislocation in physical oil flows. China’s response to the war in Iran? A crude diet, The Wall Street Journal reports : The country imported 11.6 million barrels of crude a day on average in 2025, data from the American Petroleum Institute shows. By June this year, imports had collapsed to around seven million barrels a day. China has built out a strategic oil reserve of more than 1.4 billion barrels and has deployed around 100 million barrels to plug its import gap. But it’s not just massive reserves that are serving as a cushion. While still not a massive producer, China has pushed domestic oil production up , looked to reduce oil and gas use in the chemicals sector by using coal , and worked to at-least partially wean some heavy industry off fossil fuels by using green hydrogen . And of course, the country has a wide set of policies, incentives, and subsidies intended to spur EV adoption. “China is the OPEC of oil demand,” oil analyst Homayoun Falakshahi told the paper. China could keep its imports low, match domestic demand to keep economic growth humming, and suppress global oil prices for another six months, according to the analysis firm Kpler, and still have more than 1 billion barrels in its reserves. If there is a path to peace between Washington and Tehran, it doesn’t seem likely to run through an energy crisis in Beijing.
